I have spent 26 years learning how people really talk to each other.
I began exploring communication and personal development 26 years ago. It changed how I understood relationships, empathy and responsibility, and what a single honest conversation can make possible.
My career then took me into international financial technology and commercial relationships, including years in London and Hong Kong. It was an education in ambition, performance and pressure.

Over time one question became more interesting to me than the technology or the commercial model: why do highly capable people sometimes struggle so much to work together? That question took me into full-time executive coaching.

Today I am based in Lisbon and am a founding partner of Kuma Partners. I specialise in the conversations people postpone, and in helping them address what is unspoken, rebuild trust and work together more effectively. I have not mastered human behaviour. It is more complicated than any method suggests, and I am still learning.

Years in international financial technology and commercial leadership, including London and Hong Kong, taught me how pressure shapes decisions and what delay costs. Work associated with GL Trade, SunGard, FIS and Glownet.

Vincent has explored communication and human behaviour for 26 years. After an international career in fintech and commercial leadership, he became a full-time executive coach around ten years ago and has worked with hundreds of people. He specialises in difficult conversations with founders, CEOs and leadership teams: addressing what is unspoken, rebuilding trust and working together more effectively.

What does "bridging the gap between silence and performance" mean?
It means helping people say what is going unsaid so that they can perform together.

Teams and founders often know exactly which conversation they are avoiding. The silence is costly: decisions stall, trust erodes and problems grow. I partner with founders and executives to make those conversations possible, productive and consequential.
What is a difficult conversation in a leadership context?
Any conversation where the stakes are high and the topic is uncomfortable.

Typical examples are a disagreement between co-founders, feedback about performance, a decision someone does not want to own, or a relationship that has stopped working. The difficulty is human more than informational, because people know what needs to be said.
Why do intelligent leaders postpone difficult conversations?
Because the human dynamics are complicated, whatever the person's competence.

Fear of damaging a relationship, uncertainty about the right words and the hope that the issue will resolve itself are common reasons. Postponing usually raises the cost. Preparing the conversation properly often makes it much less daunting.
I work primarily with founders, CEOs and senior leaders.
The common factor is responsibility. Clients are often facing growth, conflict, a leadership transition, a difficult decision or a situation that cannot be solved by adding another meeting.
What does executive coaching with you involve?
Confidential, challenging conversations grounded in your real leadership situation.
We look at the facts, your interpretations, what may be avoided and which action is yours to take. Sessions combine reflection with practical commitments and follow-up.
What is the difference between coaching and consulting?
Coaching strengthens your judgement and behaviour; consulting may redesign a process or organisation.

I work across the boundary when useful, but a whole-team transformation is normally better handled through Kuma Partners. We agree the scope clearly rather than making coaching a substitute for every other form of help.
Can you help with co-founder conflict?
Yes. Founder relationships and difficult executive conversations are central topics in my work.

In individual coaching, we work on your perspective, responsibility and preparation. Where the situation requires facilitated dialogue among several people, we can discuss a separate joint intervention.
Do you work with leadership teams?

How do you approach AI adoption?
I focus on the human and leadership conditions that make AI adoption useful.

Technology can improve the work, but leaders still need clarity on roles, expectations, trust, accountability and what collaboration should look like. I do not offer technical software implementation as part of personal executive coaching.
Why is emotional intelligence important in the age of AI?
Because better tools do not automatically produce better decisions between people.

Emotional intelligence includes noticing reactions, listening, dealing with disagreement and taking responsibility for the impact we have on others. These capabilities matter when technology accelerates the pace and complexity of work.

The future of work is a human question as much as a technological one.
AI is changing what people can do. I am interested in what it changes about how we work with one another: how we decide, collaborate, challenge, trust and take responsibility.

For years, companies have invested in processes, systems and productivity tools. Many still struggle with the same human obstacles: conversations that do not happen, differences that become personal and decisions that fail to translate into action.
As AI accelerates execution, the question becomes harder to ignore. What happens to a company when its technology gets faster but its people do not get better at working together?
A talk about the widening gap between what technology enables and what human relationships can sustain.
The Human Side of AI: Emotional Intelligence and the Future of Work

Imagine two capable colleagues who have stopped talking. Give them each the most powerful AI assistant in the world. Their research will improve, their proposals may become more sophisticated and they will probably move faster as individuals. Eventually, however, they will still need to speak to each other and agree what happens next.

This is the tension I explore. The future of work involves using AI more effectively and also developing the emotional maturity, responsibility and collaborative intelligence that allow people to use powerful tools well.

AI Will Not Fix a Team That Cannot Talk
, Executive Coach and Founding Partner, Kuma Partners ·

Imagine two exceptionally capable managers in the same company who no longer speak to one another. They avoid direct contact, route disagreements through colleagues and turn team meetings into careful theatre.

Now give them both an AI assistant. Each can analyse more data, write more convincing proposals and automate more of their work. Their individual productivity may rise dramatically. But the relationship between them remains exactly where it was.

This is one of the paradoxes of the AI transition. Companies are acquiring extraordinary tools for creating, analysing and executing. At the same time, they still depend on people who need to negotiate priorities, express disagreement, make commitments and live with decisions they did not choose.
AI is powerful enough. Collaboration is a separate capability, and it has to be built separately.
Individual intelligence is not collective intelligence

A group of excellent individuals does not automatically become an excellent team. People interpret the same situation differently. They protect identities, avoid embarrassment and carry assumptions about one another that rarely get tested in the open.

When nobody addresses those patterns, organisations build increasingly complicated processes around them. More meetings, approval steps and software can make the difficulty less visible. They do not necessarily remove it.

First, notice where work depends on conversations people are avoiding. The indicators are often practical: decisions repeatedly returning to the same person, messages travelling through intermediaries or agreements that disappear after a meeting.
Second, treat disagreement as information. Ask people what they see that others may not. Distinguish a disagreement about the task from a judgement about the person.
Third, make ownership explicit. A constructive conversation should produce clarity about what has been decided, what remains open and who is responsible for the next step.

Finally, give attention to how the conversation happens. People rarely do their best thinking while defending themselves. Curiosity, emotional regulation and the willingness to acknowledge one's part in a problem make serious business conversations possible.
The human side of the future of work

I am optimistic about AI. It gives people extraordinary leverage. Yet leverage amplifies what is already present. A team with trust and clear decision-making can become more capable. A team caught in avoidance may simply become faster at producing competing arguments.

The future of work therefore calls for technological fluency and an intentional investment in human intelligence: listening, candour, judgement, responsibility and the ability to move forward together.
Leaders can ask what their people can now do with AI. The harder question is what they must learn to do with one another.

The Invisible Cost of Leadership Friction
, Executive Coach and Founding Partner, Kuma Partners ·

Leadership friction rarely announces itself as a leadership problem. It often appears as slow execution, recurring meetings, departments that do not coordinate or a founder who feels that nothing moves unless they intervene.
The individuals involved may all be intelligent, competent and committed. That is what makes the situation confusing. If everyone is trying hard, why is progress so difficult?
Sometimes the missing piece is the quality of the relationships and conversations through which the plan has to travel.
The difference between agreement and alignment

Teams can agree in a meeting while leaving with different interpretations. One executive heard an ambitious target. Another heard a provisional direction. A third heard a threat to their department's resources.
The minutes record agreement. The following week, behaviour reveals something else.
Alignment takes more than saying yes to the same slide. It requires a shared understanding of priorities, trade-offs, decision rights and what happens when reality changes.

The effects can be hard to attribute. Important decisions require extra approvals. People spend time managing relationships rather than solving problems. Responsibility becomes blurred. High performers may withdraw or leave, while executives become increasingly frustrated.

Not every disagreement is harmful. In fact, constructive tension can improve a decision. The cost arises when disagreement cannot be expressed or resolved, and instead becomes avoidance, politics or passive resistance.

Start with the pattern rather than the personalities. Which decisions regularly stall? Where do handovers fail? What do people say privately that they do not say together? What is assumed to be obvious but has never been made explicit?

Then bring the right people into a conversation designed to understand the situation rather than determine who is at fault. Listen for differences in meaning, incentives and expectations. Make the disagreements visible enough to work with.
Finally, translate the conversation into behaviour. Who owns the decision? How will people raise a concern? When will the team review whether the new agreement is working?
Why it matters more in the AI era

AI will make many aspects of work faster. That does not remove the organisational cost of a delayed decision or an unresolved relationship. In some cases, it makes the contrast more obvious. The systems accelerate while the leadership team remains stuck.
For leaders, improving human coordination is part of how performance becomes possible.
